title: Sprig the Goblin and the Honest Mountain Heart
markdown:
Whispering Peaks wore snow like icing sugar. The air smelled of pine and possibility. Paths looked carved from frozen moonlight. Brooks tumbled secrets downhill as if gossip were a kind of water. Bells pealed from gargantuan peaks like a choir that had opinions about tempo and refused to be conducted.

Sprig the goblin looked a bit like a grumpy clump of moss that had sprouted ears. His nose was a touch too bulbous. His ears had wandered a mite far from usual head-proportions, as if they had set off on their own adventure and only come back for meals. His grin, when it appeared, was a sly flash. His tunic was patched in every colour, a walking rainbow that had lost a fight with a laundry basket. He smelled of damp earth and forgotten mushrooms. Underneath the unkempt, his brain buzzed like a hive of very important bees.

By his side: Peb, no average lizard. Scales of emerald, jade, peridot, a living mosaic that caught light the way a dragon’s hoard likes to be caught. He talked in chirps Sprig understood perfectly, which was fortunate, because Peb had a great many opinions and very little patience for being misunderstood.

“Lovely morning!” Peb trilled, tail twitching like a tiny happy flag. “Juicy grubs? Dew-kissed berries? A snail with an extra-slippery shell?”

Sprig’s stomach was not rumbling for grubs. It wanted a proper supper: roasted roots glistening, crumbly golden cheese like sunshine, honey-baked mushroom so sticky your fingers tingled afterward and you did not mind. His coin pouch was as empty as a winter badger burrow. Last copper: a particularly bouncy toadstool. It could reach the treetops. It did not taste like cheese. Sprig had checked. Twice.

“We need coins, Peb.” He kicked a pebble. The ice path answered with a satisfying crunch. “Good intentions do not buy supper. Neither do enthusiastic toadstools.”

Peb flicked a pink tongue. “We could sing. I do a splendid snow-owl. Hoo-hoo—”

Sprig’s ears twitched as if they wanted to leave again. “That sounds like a strangled teapot in a drainpipe. We need something that clinks.” His pebble-eyes lit. The idea arrived fully dressed, which was how Sprig’s ideas always arrived, even when they later turned out to be wearing the wrong boots. “Moonpetal blooms. Highest slopes. Alchemists pay a king’s ransom. Moonlight trapped inside. Tiny bottled stars.”

The higher slopes were not for the faint of goblin. Tricky winds snatched hats and courage with equal enthusiasm. Slippery rocks kept a personal vendetta against ankles. Things grumbled. Other things howled. A third category of thing decidedly did not appreciate visitors. The wind tugged Sprig’s mossy cap until it sat at a heroic angle that was also, unfortunately, cold.

He straightened it anyway. “Adventure. And dinner fit for a goblin king.”

They climbed. The first hour was all knees and opinions. Ice hid under pine needles and waited for ankles like a practical joke that had been planning itself since winter. Sprig’s patched tunic snagged a thorn and donated a square of yellow to the mountain, which did not say thank you. Peb rode his shoulder until a gust suggested otherwise, then scrambled ahead, a jewelled comma on grey stone, chirping back reports: loose shale, a beetle of no culinary interest, a view so large it made the empty pouch feel briefly philosophical.

Air crisped until it stung. Peb shimmered brighter, each scale a small congratulations. Pine needles whispered giggles and warnings in the same breath. Bells chimed lonely, each peal a reminder that mountains are very large and goblins are not. Sprig paused on a lip of rock to catch his important bees. Below, the village roofs were no bigger than toenails. Above, the snowfields looked edible, which was a dangerous thought for a hungry goblin.

“Still thinking of cheese?” Peb asked, kindly, as if cheese were a weather.

“I am thinking of not falling,” Sprig said. He was thinking of cheese.

On a winding path like a frozen serpent they found a crooked cottage in a hollow, as if the hollow had grown a house the way a pocket grows lint. Smoke rose in a lazy curl: cinnamon, lavender, something sparkly that made the inside of Sprig’s nose consider sneezing and then decide against it. A row of little jars sat on the sill, labelled in a handwriting that looped like ivy: fog, patience, extra Tuesday.

“It smells like warm cookies and a thunderstorm,” Peb squeaked.

“Witch Sorrel. Potent potions. More potent mischief.”

Some said she turned rocks to jelly. Others said she had an excellent recipe for spiced bog-water that tasted like hot chocolate, which was either impressive cooking or alarming magic, depending on how you felt about bogs. Through a diamond window she stirred a cauldron, grey hair braided with cobwebs like spun moonlight. She looked up as if their gaze had prickled.

“Ah, Sprig. Little Peb. Looking for the sky’s tears? Or escaping an empty larder?”

Sprig gulped. His ears flattened a polite amount. “Exploring. Majestic scenery. Perhaps a stray berry.”

Sorrel cackled like bells shaken in a jar. A soft puff of air. “Majestic scenery hides majestic treasures. Beware those who guard them too closely. Some shepherds are more observant than they appear. Eyes like icicles. Faces like frozen lakes.” She winked. Purple smoke: lavender and mint. It tickled.

They climbed on, her words mixing with the mint until Sprig could not tell which was the warning and which was the flavour. Steeper. Narrower. The path demanded careful footwork and then demanded it again, because mountains enjoy repeating themselves. A raven watched them with the professional interest of someone who had seen goblins come up hungry and go down wiser, or not come down at all. Peb did an experimental snow-owl for the raven. The raven left. Sprig did not blame it.

Then, on a rocky outcrop against impossibly blue sky: an ogre.

Not roaring. Pastoral. Knitted fleece vest in a muted brown that had never tried to be fashionable. Crooked crook of gnarled mountain wood. Enormous kind eyes. Enormous in general. Dinner-plate hands. Boulder feet. Humming, slightly off-key, among woolly sheep like soft clouds that had learned to walk.

“An ogre shepherd,” Sprig whispered. “Rather peaceful.”

Grungle blinked earth-brown eyes, the colour of warm ground after rain. “Hello, little ones. Lost? Or admiring the view?”

Sprig puffed. Bravery, he had found, could be inflated like a balloon if you blew hard enough and did not look at the pin. “Not lost. Seeking Moonpetals. Essence of moonlight!”

Grungle nodded, slow, and went back to humming, more interested in sheep than goblins. The sheep agreed with this priority. One of them wore a little knitted bell, slightly off-key, as if it had taken lessons from its shepherd. Sprig’s confidence surged. Easy. An ogre who hummed was an ogre who would not notice a creative bargain. They scrambled higher, eyes greedy for silver, past a scatter of bones that were only branches and a shadow that was only a cloud, and found a hidden patch: white petals shimmering as if they had drunk a stream of moonlight and decided to keep it. A few steps farther, if Sprig had bothered to look, the rock darkened toward a mouth of a den, but Sprig was looking at pretty, and pretty is a loud colour.

Sprig gathered a careful bunch. The blooms were cool. They made his patched pockets look suddenly important.

He approached again, Peb an anxious gargoyle on his shoulder, scales shifting through nervous greens. “Master Shepherd! Magnificent Moonpetals! Trade for those juicy mountain berries in your satchel?”

Grungle’s gaze took in the eager grin, Peb’s colour-shift, the way Sprig’s empty pouch still managed to look hopeful. Then he smiled, slow, rumbling, crinkling. “Moonpetals. Fine. Rare. But they only truly flourish near the old troll’s den. The troll is fond of shiny things. He might think you’ve stolen them. Not known for forgiving.”

Sprig froze. He had not seen a den. He had seen pretty and called it done. Peb chirped alarm, a small bright sound that did not help the stomach.

“And those tasty berries,” Grungle continued, amused, “are bog-buds. Bitter. Sour. Not a goblin’s supper.” A tree-branch finger pointed at deep purple moss in softer sun. “Moonpetals thrive there, away from the troll. Easier. Safer. Soil’s just right.”

Sprig’s jaw dropped. The ogre had seen the half-truth, the snack mistake, and the better patch Sprig had meant to keep as a professional secret. Cheeks went goblin-green, which on a goblin is a serious shade.

A gust of cinnamon, lavender, mint. Sorrel shimmered out of the air as if the mountain had been keeping her in a pocket. “Hello, Grungle! Still playing hide-and-seek with the truth, Sprig? He thought bog-buds were berries!”

Grungle chuckled. Sheep lifted their heads, considered the joke, and returned to grass. “This young goblin is trying to earn supper. Shy about empty coin. Thought creative trading might work.”

Sprig slumped. The plan unravelled like a cheap sweater on a bramble. All those important bees in his brain sat down at once. “I just wanted a proper meal.”

Sorrel’s glint softened, though mischief stayed on duty. “No shame in that. Honesty, as Grungle has shown, is often the quickest path to the finest fare. Mountain-detective, this one.”

Grungle waved a wagon-wheel hand. “Pride is a heavy burden up a mountain. Heavier than Moonpetals.” From the satchel: plump ruby berries, the real kind, so red they looked like a jewellery shop had decided to be edible, and a round golden cheese that smelled of a proper creamery, the sort of smell that makes empty pouches feel less tragic. “Take these. For your honesty. Next time, ask. I’m not as fearsome as I look. Easier than pulling wool over my eyes.”

Sorrel dusted the food with a shimmer. Extra tastiness, from a pantry that probably contained thunderstorms. “Go on. Enjoy.”

They went down with Moonpetals still in hand and supper that clinked in a different way. The path that had been all knees became, mysteriously, all downhill opinions, which is easier on pockets. Bells turned cheerful, as if the choir had found the right page. Once they passed the cottage, a puff of mint followed them like a wink that had learned to walk.

They sat on a flat stone above the village and divided the food with the seriousness of a treaty. Peb declared the cheese absolutely scrumptious, which from Peb was a review with stars. The berries stained Sprig’s fingers jewel-red. The Moonpetals in his other hand kept their cool bottled-star glow, ready for an alchemist who paid in actual coins, which suddenly felt like a bonus rather than a scheme.

Sprig’s pouch was still light. His supper was not. The peaks kept their icing-sugar snow. The goblin, for once, did not try to bounce a toadstool in payment, and the important bees in his head, after a long conference, agreed that asking had been the cleverest plan of the day.
characters: Sprig (patchwork goblin with empty pockets), Peb (jewel-scaled lizard companion), Sorrel (witch of cinnamon and mint)
audience: children aged 9-10, amusing distant-lands fantasy for independent readers
author: StoryGen Community
